correctness.rationale: For all distinct odd primes p<q, a,b≥1: multiplicative σ/n bounds prove deficiency for p≥7, for p=5,q≥17, and for p=5,q∈{11,13} with a=1. For p=3, 6 divides n. The only remaining squarefree case 70 is abundant but the omitted proper-divisor sum 4 is impossible. Four exact complementary-divisor sums (350:44,490:46,550:16,650:2) establish semiperfect seeds; all remaining configurations are their multiples. Proper-divisor and deficiency checks give the primitive part. The 550-case computation only supports, never replaces, the unrestricted proof.

evidence: Amato–Hasler–Melfi–Parton arXiv:1802.07178, abstract, introduction, Theorem 4.7 and Sections 2–4: they classify or enumerate primitive abundant/weird phenomena in various bounded total multiplicities and discuss global unknowns; Theorem 4.7 excludes certain primitive weird numbers only when Ω is bounded by seven.

Dickson 1913 is cited in that paper as a classification of primitive abundant numbers with restricted prime-support size after fixing the 2-adic exponent; this pertains to abundance, not a general semiperfectness decision. The original older full text was not inspected.
broader_coverage.reasoning: A bound on prime factors counted with multiplicity cannot settle all exponents. Primitive abundant number classification does not by itself determine which abundant numbers have a distinct proper-divisor representation; furthermore our assertion covers nonprimitive semiperfect numbers and weirdness.

value.rationale: Semiperfectness is a natural integer divisor-subset-sum property; determining it on an entire unbounded three-prime family is a motivated classification rather than a fixed cutoff. It identifies four minimal semiperfect generators and proves that 70 is the sole weird exception. The already-known examples are explicitly credited; the universal characterization supplies the additional structural fact.
